q: Situation: A bank customer reports that an ATM has retained his debit card. Courses of action: I. Block the card immediately and issue a replacement after verification. II. Ask the customer to wait several days without taking any action.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: The card should be blocked promptly to prevent misuse and a replacement can be issued after verification. Waiting without action is unsafe.

q: Situation: An employee notices that a printer in the office is not working. Courses of action: I. Check basic connections and restart the printer if appropriate. II. Immediately replace the printer without checking the problem.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Basic troubleshooting should be attempted before replacing equipment. Immediate replacement without diagnosis is unnecessary.

q: Situation: A customer finds an unauthorized transaction on her bank account. Courses of action: I. Report the transaction promptly to the bank and request investigation. II. Ignore it unless more unauthorized transactions occur.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: An unauthorized transaction should be reported immediately so that the account can be protected and the transaction investigated.

q: Situation: A student has an important examination tomorrow but has not yet prepared the entire syllabus. Courses of action: I. Prioritize important topics and study systematically. II. Stop studying completely because the entire syllabus cannot be completed.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Focusing on high-priority topics is practical. Giving up entirely is not a constructive response.

q: Situation: A shop notices that a refrigerator is making an unusual noise. Courses of action: I. Have the refrigerator inspected by a qualified technician. II. Continue using it indefinitely without checking the cause.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: An unusual mechanical sound may indicate a fault, so inspection is sensible. Ignoring it indefinitely is inappropriate.

q: Situation: Heavy rain is forecast while a family is planning a picnic in an open park. Courses of action: I. Consider postponing or shifting the picnic indoors. II. Proceed without any backup plan regardless of the forecast.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Considering a safer alternative in light of the forecast is prudent. Proceeding without any contingency is not.

q: Situation: A customer forgets the PIN of her debit card. Courses of action: I. Follow the bank's approved PIN-reset procedure after identity verification. II. Ask another customer to tell her the PIN.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Identity verification and the formal reset process protect the customer's account. Sharing or guessing PIN information is improper.

q: Situation: A passenger realizes that he has left his wallet in a taxi. Courses of action: I. Contact the taxi service or driver and report the loss promptly. II. Share the wallet's full details publicly on social media without checking with the taxi service.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Reporting the loss through the service or driver is a sensible first step. Publicly exposing personal details can create privacy and security risks.

q: Situation: A bank branch receives a large number of customers just before closing time. Courses of action: I. Manage the queue systematically and serve customers according to branch procedures. II. Close the branch immediately and ask everyone to leave without considering the queue.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: The branch should manage customers fairly and according to procedure. Abruptly abandoning customers is not proper.

q: Situation: A student sees a classmate using notes during a closed-book examination. Courses of action: I. Inform the invigilator privately. II. Publicly confront and embarrass the classmate during the examination.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Reporting suspected cheating to the responsible authority is appropriate. Public confrontation may disrupt the examination and is not the proper procedure.

q: Situation: An office receives an email containing a suspicious attachment from an unknown sender. Courses of action: I. Avoid opening the attachment and report the email to the IT/security team. II. Open the attachment on a shared office computer to find out what it contains.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Suspicious attachments should not be opened. Reporting them to security or IT is the proper course.

q: Situation: A customer is unable to complete an online bank transfer because the service is temporarily unavailable. Courses of action: I. Check whether the bank has reported a system outage and retry later. II. Repeatedly enter incorrect transaction details hoping the transfer will succeed.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Checking for an outage and retrying later is sensible. Entering incorrect information repeatedly is risky and improper.

q: Situation: A resident notices water leaking continuously from a public pipe. Courses of action: I. Report the leak to the relevant municipal authority. II. Ignore it because the pipe does not belong to the resident.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Reporting the leak can prevent water loss and further damage. Ignoring a known public problem is not proper.

q: Situation: An employee receives a complaint that a colleague is repeatedly arriving late. Courses of action: I. Verify the facts and, if necessary, address the issue through the proper supervisory process. II. Immediately post the colleague's attendance details in a public group chat.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: The complaint should be verified and handled through appropriate channels. Publicly exposing attendance details is unprofessional.

q: Situation: A bank branch's token-display system stops working during a busy period. Courses of action: I. Use an approved manual queue system while arranging technical support. II. Allow customers to serve themselves without any queue system.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: An approved manual queue can maintain orderly service during a technical failure. Allowing customers to serve themselves would create confusion.

q: Situation: A sales team repeatedly misses monthly targets. Courses of action: I. Review performance data and identify the main causes of the shortfall. II. Replace all team members immediately without investigating the reasons for poor performance.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: The management should first identify whether the problem is skills, resources, market conditions, or execution. Immediate replacement without analysis is unjustified.

q: Situation: A bank branch receives several customer complaints about unusually long waiting times. Courses of action: I. Analyze the queue and staffing pattern during peak hours. II. Add temporary staff or redesign the service process if the analysis supports it.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Both diagnosing the bottleneck and taking an evidence-based corrective step are appropriate responses.

q: Situation: An employee repeatedly submits reports with avoidable errors despite previous feedback. Courses of action: I. Provide specific corrective guidance and review the next report closely. II. If errors continue, consider formal performance-management measures according to policy.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Progressive action is appropriate: clarify expectations first and escalate through formal procedures if the problem persists. Both actions are proper.

q: Situation: A branch discovers that several loan applications contain missing documents. Courses of action: I. Return the applications with a clear list of required documents. II. Approve the loans anyway to avoid delaying business.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Required documentation must be completed before approval. Approving incomplete applications simply to save time is improper.

q: Situation: A project is behind schedule because two teams depend on each other's work but have conflicting priorities. Courses of action: I. Hold a coordination meeting and clarify dependencies and deadlines. II. Ask both teams to continue working independently without changing anything.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: The problem is coordination-based, so clarifying dependencies and deadlines is appropriate. Continuing without adjustment is unlikely to solve it.

q: Situation: A bank employee accidentally sends a customer statement to the wrong email address. Courses of action: I. Report the incident immediately through the bank's data-security process. II. Attempt to contain the disclosure and contact the unintended recipient through approved procedures.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: A data disclosure requires prompt internal reporting and appropriate containment or recovery measures. Both actions are proper.

q: Situation: A manager learns that two employees are in conflict and their disagreement is affecting team output. Courses of action: I. Meet the employees and understand the issue before deciding on a resolution. II. Transfer one employee immediately without hearing either side.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Understanding both sides before taking action is fair and likely to produce a durable solution. Immediate transfer without inquiry is premature.

q: Situation: A branch's digital customer-service channel receives many repetitive questions. Courses of action: I. Build a searchable FAQ or automated response system for routine questions. II. Continue requiring every employee to answer each routine question manually.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Automating repetitive queries can improve efficiency and free staff for more complex cases. Continuing the same manual workload is less efficient.

q: Situation: A new branch employee is performing well technically but frequently misses deadlines because priorities are unclear. Courses of action: I. Set clear priorities and deadlines. II. Criticize the employee for being slow without clarifying expectations.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: The stated cause is unclear priorities, so clarifying them is the appropriate remedy. Criticism without guidance is not constructive.

q: Situation: A company receives a credible report that an important supplier may be unable to deliver critical materials next month. Courses of action: I. Verify the supplier's position and assess the likely impact. II. Identify backup suppliers or contingency arrangements if the risk is confirmed.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: The organization should first verify the risk and then prepare contingency measures if necessary. Both actions are proper.

q: Situation: A bank sees a rise in failed digital transactions after a software update. Courses of action: I. Examine transaction logs and involve the technology team to identify the cause. II. Roll back the update immediately without checking whether the update caused the failures.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: The issue should be diagnosed first. An immediate rollback without evidence could create new problems.

q: Situation: A team member proposes purchasing expensive software to solve a reporting problem. Courses of action: I. Evaluate the existing tools and compare costs and benefits before purchasing. II. Approve the purchase immediately because expensive software is likely to be better.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: A cost-benefit and existing-capability review is appropriate. Price alone does not establish suitability.

q: Situation: An employee complains that a new workplace rule is unfair. Courses of action: I. Review the rule, its purpose, and how it is being applied. II. Reject the complaint immediately because management created the rule.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: The complaint deserves an objective review. Management decisions should not be treated as automatically correct without examination.

q: Situation: A bank notices that customers are frequently abandoning a digital account-opening process midway. Courses of action: I. Analyze where users drop out and identify obstacles. II. Remove all verification steps immediately to maximize completion.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: The abandonment points should first be analyzed. Removing essential verification without understanding its purpose could create security and compliance problems.

q: Situation: A manager must decide whether to approve overtime for a team facing a sudden workload increase. Courses of action: I. Assess urgency, workload, available staff, and budget before approving overtime. II. Approve unlimited overtime immediately so that the workload disappears as quickly as possible.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: A balanced decision should consider the workload, urgency, available alternatives, and cost. Unlimited overtime without assessment is inappropriate.

q: Situation: A bank's fraud-monitoring system flags a high-value transaction that differs sharply from a customer's normal activity, but the transaction could also be legitimate. Courses of action: I. Immediately treat the transaction as fraud and permanently close the customer's account. II. Conduct enhanced verification and investigation before deciding whether to block or release the transaction.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: The unusual transaction justifies enhanced verification, but permanent closure without investigation is excessive. Only II is proper.

q: Situation: A bank discovers that a senior employee has approved several unusually large loans that bypassed normal checks. Courses of action: I. Preserve records and initiate an independent investigation. II. Ignore the issue because the employee has a strong performance record.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Potential control breaches require evidence preservation and independent investigation. Past performance does not justify ignoring suspicious activity.

q: Situation: A company is considering closing a branch that has low profitability but serves an area with many customers who have limited digital access. Courses of action: I. Evaluate profitability together with customer needs, strategic value, and alternatives before deciding. II. Close the branch immediately because low profitability alone proves it is unnecessary.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: A branch decision should consider both financial and service factors. Profitability alone does not conclusively establish that closure is appropriate.

q: Situation: A company suspects that confidential product information has been leaked by an employee, but there is no conclusive evidence. Courses of action: I. Secure relevant systems and investigate access records while preserving due process. II. Publicly accuse the suspected employee to discourage others from leaking information.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Evidence should be secured and the matter investigated fairly. Public accusation without proof is inappropriate and potentially damaging.

q: Situation: A bank's automated credit model starts rejecting a much higher proportion of applications after a system change. Preliminary evidence suggests a possible model error, but the extent is unknown. Courses of action: I. Audit the model and affected decisions to identify the cause and scope. II. Continue using the model without review until enough customers complain.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: A significant unexpected change in outcomes requires prompt validation and impact assessment. Waiting for complaints would be irresponsible.

q: Situation: A company faces a cyberattack that disrupts some internal systems, but customer-facing services are still operating. Courses of action: I. Isolate affected systems and activate the incident-response plan. II. Publicly disclose every technical detail immediately, before the investigation establishes what happened.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Containment and incident response should begin immediately. Public disclosure should be accurate, coordinated, and based on verified information rather than speculation.

q: Situation: A manager must choose between two projects because the team has capacity for only one. Project A offers high potential revenue but high uncertainty; Project B offers moderate revenue with strong strategic fit and lower risk. Courses of action: I. Compare expected returns, strategic value, risk, and resource requirements before deciding. II. Automatically choose Project A because its potential revenue is higher.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: A balanced decision requires considering return, risk, strategic fit, and resources. Potential revenue alone is insufficient.

q: Situation: A customer alleges discriminatory treatment by a bank employee, but the employee denies the allegation. Courses of action: I. Obtain statements and relevant records and investigate impartially. II. Immediately dismiss the employee solely because the allegation was made.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: A serious allegation warrants prompt, impartial investigation. Disciplinary action should follow evidence and due process rather than the allegation alone.

q: Situation: A bank is planning a major change to its digital lending process. Pilot data show faster processing but also a modest increase in customer complaints. Courses of action: I. Analyze the complaints and pilot outcomes before scaling the change. II. Roll out the new process nationwide immediately because processing is faster.
opts: Only course of action I is proper
Only course of action II is proper
Both I and II are proper
Neither I nor II is proper
exp: Both efficiency and customer impact matter. The complaints should be understood before a full rollout; speed alone is not sufficient justification.
